screens.title: Advanced Exception Handling & RAII
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how modern C++ uses two complementary ideas — the noexcept contract and the RAII idiom — to make error paths safe and efficient. First, we will define what it means for a function to be declared noexcept and why breaking that promise leads to program termination. Then we will walk through stack unwinding, the automatic process that destroys local objects when an exception propagates. That mechanism is the reason RAII works: if a constructor acquires a resource and the destructor releases it, resources are reliably cleaned up during unwinding. You will see concrete code examples that illustrate non-RAII resource leaks, RAII wrappers using smart pointers, and a starter exercise to implement a FileLocker RAII class. Along the way we will highlight practical best practices—mark move operations noexcept when possible, prefer std::unique_ptr for sole ownership, and never let destructors propagate exceptions. By the end of this chapter you will understand the runtime guarantees that make RAII and noexcept so valuable, and you will be prepared to modify non-RAII code to use smart pointers and RAII wrappers.

Advanced Exception Handling & RAII
Practical patterns to ensure your C++ programs clean up resources reliably and run efficiently when errors occur.
In this lesson
Understand noexcept, stack unwinding, RAII, smart pointers, and destructor safety.
Practical code examples and a FileLocker activity prepare you to apply these patterns in real projects.
Why it matters
Correct resource cleanup prevents leaks and undefined states; noexcept enables important performance optimizations in containers.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives frame practical skills you will practice. First, you will understand the noexcept specifier: what it promises, how violating it leads to termination, and why it matters for performance. Second, you will explain stack unwinding: how destructors of automatic objects are called in reverse order when an exception propagates, and how that guarantees cleanup when used with RAII. Third, you will master the RAII idiom: tying resource acquisition to construction and release to destruction so that exceptions cannot leak resources. Finally on this screen, you will begin applying smart pointers like unique_ptr and shared_ptr as RAII wrappers to ensure dynamic memory and other resources are freed reliably. Each of these objectives includes a short skill description and a competency milestone so you can verify your understanding as you work through the hands-on FileLocker exercise later in the chapter.

screens.title: The noexcept specifier
screens.narratorSegment: The noexcept specifier is a contract you add to a function signature to promise it will not throw an exception. That promise does two things: it documents intent for other developers, and it lets the compiler optimize. When a function is declared noexcept the runtime can avoid generating some of the bookkeeping code required for exception propagation, which can improve performance especially in move operations. However, that promise is strict: if a noexcept function actually throws, the C++ runtime will call std::terminate and the process will end. Consider the difference between a helper function that simply manipulates data and one that performs input and output; only use noexcept when you can guarantee no exceptions escape. A concrete example is move constructors used by containers: when an object's move constructor is noexcept, std::vector can move elements during reallocation instead of copying, which is faster. A common misconception is that noexcept suppresses exceptions — it does not. It is a compile-time and runtime contract, not an error-handling mechanism. When designing APIs, prefer noexcept for destructors and for move operations that are implemented in a non-throwing way. Takeaway: use noexcept to express guaranteed non-throwing behavior, but be careful — if you accidentally throw through that boundary, the program terminates. How will you decide which of your move operations can safely be marked noexcept?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › The noexcept specifier
noexcept: a non-throwing contract
Declare functions that are guaranteed not to throw, and enable runtime and container optimizations.
Definition
A function declared noexcept promises no exceptions will escape. If one does, std::terminate() is called.
Concrete example
Mark a move constructor noexcept so containers can move elements instead of copying during reallocation, improving performance.
Common misconception
noexcept does not suppress exceptions. It is a promise; violating it causes termination, not recovery.
<!-- Example adapted from chapter content --> #include <iostream> #include <stdexcept> void doSomethingNonThrowing() noexcept { std::cout << "Inside doSomethingNonThrowing." << std::endl; // throwing here would call std::terminate() } void doSomethingPotentiallyThrowing(int value) { if (value < 0) { throw std::runtime_error("Negative value encountered."); } std::cout << "Working with value: " << value << std::endl; } // If doSomethingNonThrowing threw, the program would terminate.
Key Takeaway

Use noexcept when you can guarantee no exceptions and you want clearer intent and better performance.

Pro tip
Prefer noexcept for destructors and for move operations that do not allocate or throw.

screens.title: noexcept and performance in containers
screens.narratorSegment: When standard library containers like vector grow, they may reallocate storage and move or copy elements into the new memory. The container prefers move operations because they can transfer ownership with less work than copying, but it will only prefer moving when the move constructor is non-throwing or declared noexcept. Marking a move constructor noexcept is therefore a performance decision as well as a correctness contract. In practice you follow a small decision process: first, implement the move so it does not throw (for example, avoid allocations during move); second, declare it noexcept; third, test that moving does not produce exceptions. A concrete scenario: if your type holds a pointer and the move just swaps pointers, that move is typically non-throwing and should be noexcept. A misconception to avoid is believing noexcept will make a throwing move magically safe — it will not. If you mark a move noexcept and it throws, the program will terminate. Takeaway: design move operations for non-throwing behavior when they are used by containers, and mark them noexcept to unlock move-based optimizations. noexcept and performance in containers means declaring move operations noexcept gives containers permission to move objects during reallocation, often improving performance.. In practical terms, how noexcept on moves enables efficient reallocation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › noexcept and performance
Decision process for noexcept moves
Follow these steps to allow containers to prefer moves safely.
1. Implement move to avoid throwing operations, like allocations.
2. Mark the move constructor noexcept when it is safe.
3. Run tests that exercise reallocation to catch unintended exceptions.
Concrete example
If a move just swaps internal pointers and does no allocations, it can and should be noexcept so std::vector will move elements during growth rather than copy them.
Misconception
noexcept makes code safer from exceptions — incorrect. It enforces a contract and will terminate if violated.
Why it matters
Containers can prefer moving elements across reallocation only when moves are noexcept, improving runtime efficiency and reducing copies.

screens.title: Stack Unwinding
screens.narratorSegment: Stack unwinding is the runtime process that runs destructors for automatic objects as an exception is propagated up the call stack in search of a matching handler. When an exception is thrown, the runtime examines each stack frame between the throw point and the eventual catch and invokes destructors for objects constructed in those frames in reverse order of construction. This guarantees that resources owned by well-written objects are released, which is the basis for RAII. For a concrete example use the provided MyResource class. If one resource throws while doing work, destructors for previously constructed resources still run and perform their cleanup. A frequent misconception is thinking that raw pointers will be freed automatically; they will not. Only objects with destructors that perform cleanup are invoked during unwinding. In the example, unique_ptr instances hold resources and ensure their destructors call delete. The key takeaway: design destructors to be safe and to perform necessary cleanup because stack unwinding depends on them to keep your program in a valid state. How might you refactor code that currently uses raw new/delete to rely on RAII instead?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Stack Unwinding
What is stack unwinding?
It is the process that destroys automatic objects as an exception moves up the call stack.
Definition
Destructors for local objects are invoked in reverse order of construction until a catch block is found.
Concrete example
If a local resource's method throws, previously constructed resources still have their destructors executed, freeing handles or memory.
// MyResource example (conceptual) class MyResource { public: MyResource(int id) : id_(id) { std::cout << "Acquired " << id_ << std::endl; } ~MyResource() { std::cout << "Released " << id_ << std::endl; } void doWork() { if (id_ == 2) throw std::runtime_error("Error in resource 2"); } private: int id_; }; // When doWork() throws, destructors for constructed objects are run during unwinding.
Misconception
Raw pointers are not automatically freed during unwinding; objects with destructors are.
Key Takeaway

Design resources as objects with safe destructors so stack unwinding reliably releases them.

screens.title: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (RAII)
screens.narratorSegment: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization, or RAII, is the C++ idiom that binds resource lifetime to object lifetime: a constructor acquires a resource and the destructor releases it. Because destructors run during stack unwinding, RAII ensures resources are freed both in normal control flow and when exceptions occur. A common example is file handling: if you open a file and then an exception occurs before you call close, a correctly designed RAII object such as std::fstream or a custom wrapper will close the file in its destructor. The counterexample is manual open and close calls with raw pointers or C file handles — when an exception occurs, the close call may never run and the resource leaks. Use RAII for memory using smart pointers, for locks using lock-guard objects, and for temporary OS resources using small wrapper classes. A common pitfall is writing destructors that can throw; destructors should catch and handle errors internally, perhaps logging failures but not propagating exceptions. Takeaway: prefer RAII everywhere you manage resources so exception paths remain safe and predictable. Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (RAII) means acquire resources in constructors and release them in destructors so cleanup is automatic, even on exceptions.. In practical terms, an idiom for reliable resource management. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › RAII
RAII: resource lifetime equals object lifetime
Wrap resources in objects whose destructors release them so cleanup is automatic.
Non-RAII risk
Manual close calls can be skipped when exceptions occur, leading to leaks.
RAII example
std::fstream and smart pointers are RAII types that free resources in their destructors.
File handling example (non-RAII)
void processFile(const std::string& filename) {
  FILE* file = fopen(filename.c_str(), "r");
  if (!file) throw std::runtime_error("Failed to open file.");
  // If an exception is thrown before fclose, file is leaked.
  fclose(file);
}
Key Takeaway

Prefer RAII wrappers so resources are freed automatically during normal execution and stack unwinding.

Pro tip
If an operation in a destructor can fail, handle the failure internally; do not throw.

screens.title: Non-RAII vs RAII: file handling
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing non-RAII and RAII file handling shows clearly why RAII is preferred. In the non-RAII example you open a file with a raw FILE* and call fclose when you're done. If an exception occurs between the open and close calls, the close call may never execute, and the file handle leaks. In contrast, a RAII wrapper like std::fstream or a custom wrapper opens the file in the constructor and closes it in the destructor. Because destructors are executed during stack unwinding, the file will be closed whether the function finishes normally or an exception propagates. A concrete contrast: imagine a function that performs several operations after opening a file and one of those operations throws. With RAII the file is closed automatically; without RAII it is not. A common misunderstanding is believing that simply adding try/catch around the function will fix leaks — it may, but it complicates code and risks missing other exit paths. RAII centralizes cleanup logic and reduces error-prone bookkeeping. Takeaway: convert manual resource management to RAII to make error handling simpler and safer. Non-RAII vs RAII: file handling means raii centralizes cleanup in destructors so resources are released reliably, while manual open/close is error-prone in the presence of exceptions.. In practical terms, why raii prevents leaks when exceptions occur. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Non-RAII vs RAII
Non-RAII file handling
void processFile(const std::string& filename) {
  FILE* file = fopen(filename.c_str(), "r");
  if (!file) throw std::runtime_error("Failed to open file.");
  // ... complex logic that may throw ...
  fclose(file); // may be skipped if an exception occurs
}
Risk
Leaks and stale file handles when exceptions interrupt the normal close call.
RAII approach
Use std::fstream or a custom wrapper whose destructor calls close, so the file is closed even if an exception occurs.
Benefit
Automatic, central cleanup that is reliable during both normal control flow and exceptions.

screens.title: Smart pointers as RAII wrappers
screens.narratorSegment: Smart pointers are standard RAII types that manage dynamic memory and free it when the owning object is destroyed. std::unique_ptr models exclusive ownership: only one unique_ptr owns the resource at a time, and its destructor calls delete. Because unique_ptr's destructor runs during stack unwinding, it automatically frees memory even if an exception is thrown. std::shared_ptr models shared ownership: it maintains a reference count and destroys the managed object when the last shared_ptr goes out of scope. A concrete example is creating MyResource instances with std::make_unique; when an exception occurs later, the unique_ptr's destructor invokes delete so memory is reclaimed. A common misconception is that shared_ptr always adds overhead you must avoid; while it has some cost, shared ownership is the right tool for some designs. Another pitfall is mixing raw delete calls with smart pointers — do not manage the same resource with both patterns. Key takeaway: prefer unique_ptr for single ownership and shared_ptr when multiple parts of a program must share a resource, and trust their destructors to provide automatic cleanup in the presence of exceptions. Smart pointers as RAII wrappers means use unique_ptr for exclusive ownership and shared_ptr for shared ownership; both provide raii-based cleanup during stack unwinding.. In practical terms, how std::unique_ptr and std::shared_ptr manage ownership. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Smart pointers
Smart pointers implement RAII
unique_ptr for exclusive ownership, shared_ptr for shared ownership; both call delete when their lifetime ends.
std::unique_ptr
Exclusive ownership; destructor calls delete on the managed pointer when it goes out of scope.
std::shared_ptr
Shared ownership; resource is destroyed when the last owner is destroyed.
Concrete usage
std::unique_ptr<MyResource> res = std::make_unique<MyResource>(1);
res->doWork(); // If exception is thrown, res's destructor still runs and deletes the object.

std::shared_ptr<MyResource> s1 = std::make_shared<MyResource>(2);
{
  auto s2 = s1; // shared ownership, destructor runs when last shared_ptr is destroyed
}
Key Takeaway

screens.title: Destructors and Exceptions
screens.narratorSegment: Destructors should generally not throw exceptions. If a destructor throws while another exception is already active—meaning unwinding is in progress—the C++ runtime will call std::terminate and abruptly end the program. This makes throwing from destructors dangerous because it defeats the cleanup guarantees and prevents graceful recovery. Modern C++ implicitly treats destructors as noexcept unless explicitly declared otherwise, which enforces this safety discipline. If a destructor must perform an operation that can fail, handle the failure inside the destructor: log the error, set an internal error state, or swallow the failure quietly in a controlled way. A concrete problematic scenario is calling cleanup code that throws a network error during unwinding; the result would be termination, not an exception you can catch. A common misconception is thinking you can rely on destructor exceptions to propagate useful error information; you cannot. Takeaway: implement destructors to complete non-throwing cleanup, and move any fallible operations to places where failures can be handled without risking termination. screens.title: Common pitfalls and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: This checklist gathers common pitfalls and recommended practices for exception-safe C++ code. First, prefer RAII: encapsulate resources in objects whose destructors perform cleanup. Second, use smart pointers for dynamic memory: std::unique_ptr for exclusive ownership, std::shared_ptr when shared semantics are needed. Third, mark destructors noexcept so termination does not occur unexpectedly, and ensure destructors catch and handle internal failures rather than throwing. Fourth, declare move constructors and move assignment noexcept when they do not throw to enable container optimizations. Fifth, avoid mixing raw new/delete with smart pointers and avoid double-management of resources. Sixth, write tests that simulate exceptions during construction and mid-operation so you can confirm cleanup runs during unwinding. A common misconception is that wrapping everything in try/catch everywhere is the right answer — it is not. Instead, design types with strong RAII semantics and let stack unwinding and destructors reliably clean up. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the three most important concepts you should carry forward. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how modern C++ uses two complementary ideas — the noexcept contract and the RAII idiom — to make error paths safe and efficient. First, we will define what it means for a function to be declared noexcept and why breaking that promise leads to program termination. Then we will walk through stack unwinding, the automatic process that destroys local objects when an exception propagates. That mechanism is the reason RAII works: if a constructor acquires a resource and the destructor releases it, resources are reliably cleaned up during unwinding. You will see concrete code examples that illustrate non-RAII resource leaks, RAII wrappers using smart pointers, and a starter exercise to implement a FileLocker RAII class. Along the way we will highlight practical best practices—mark move operations noexcept when possible, prefer std::unique_ptr for sole ownership, and never let destructors propagate exceptions. By the end of this chapter you will understand the runtime guarantees that make RAII and noexcept so valuable, and you will be prepared to modify non-RAII code to use smart pointers and RAII wrappers.

These learning objectives frame practical skills you will practice. First, you will understand the noexcept specifier: what it promises, how violating it leads to termination, and why it matters for performance. Second, you will explain stack unwinding: how destructors of automatic objects are called in reverse order when an exception propagates, and how that guarantees cleanup when used with RAII. Third, you will master the RAII idiom: tying resource acquisition to construction and release to destruction so that exceptions cannot leak resources. Finally on this screen, you will begin applying smart pointers like unique_ptr and shared_ptr as RAII wrappers to ensure dynamic memory and other resources are freed reliably. Each of these objectives includes a short skill description and a competency milestone so you can verify your understanding as you work through the hands-on FileLocker exercise later in the chapter.

We continue with complementary objectives that focus on safety and subtle pitfalls. First, you will identify common mistakes such as throwing exceptions from destructors and understand why that leads to immediate termination during unwinding. Second, you will learn to prefer noexcept on move constructors and move assignment to enable container optimizations, especially in standard containers like vector. Third, you will practice designing RAII wrappers beyond memory: files, locks, and temporary system resources should be managed by objects whose destructors perform non-throwing cleanup. Fourth, you'll be able to interpret a starter FileLocker exercise: implement an RAII lock that throws a LockAcquisitionException on contention and releases the lock without throwing in the destructor. Together these skills let you reason about error paths, write predictable cleanup code, and avoid undefined states in the face of exceptions.

The noexcept specifier is a contract you add to a function signature to promise it will not throw an exception. That promise does two things: it documents intent for other developers, and it lets the compiler optimize. When a function is declared noexcept the runtime can avoid generating some of the bookkeeping code required for exception propagation, which can improve performance especially in move operations. However, that promise is strict: if a noexcept function actually throws, the C++ runtime will call std::terminate and the process will end. Consider the difference between a helper function that simply manipulates data and one that performs input and output; only use noexcept when you can guarantee no exceptions escape. A concrete example is move constructors used by containers: when an object's move constructor is noexcept, std::vector can move elements during reallocation instead of copying, which is faster. A common misconception is that noexcept suppresses exceptions — it does not. It is a compile-time and runtime contract, not an error-handling mechanism. When designing APIs, prefer noexcept for destructors and for move operations that are implemented in a non-throwing way. Takeaway: use noexcept to express guaranteed non-throwing behavior, but be careful — if you accidentally throw through that boundary, the program terminates. How will you decide which of your move operations can safely be marked noexcept?

When standard library containers like vector grow, they may reallocate storage and move or copy elements into the new memory. The container prefers move operations because they can transfer ownership with less work than copying, but it will only prefer moving when the move constructor is non-throwing or declared noexcept. Marking a move constructor noexcept is therefore a performance decision as well as a correctness contract. In practice you follow a small decision process: first, implement the move so it does not throw (for example, avoid allocations during move); second, declare it noexcept; third, test that moving does not produce exceptions. A concrete scenario: if your type holds a pointer and the move just swaps pointers, that move is typically non-throwing and should be noexcept. A misconception to avoid is believing noexcept will make a throwing move magically safe — it will not. If you mark a move noexcept and it throws, the program will terminate. Takeaway: design move operations for non-throwing behavior when they are used by containers, and mark them noexcept to unlock move-based optimizations. noexcept and performance in containers means declaring move operations noexcept gives containers permission to move objects during reallocation, often improving performance.. In practical terms, how noexcept on moves enables efficient reallocation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Stack unwinding is the runtime process that runs destructors for automatic objects as an exception is propagated up the call stack in search of a matching handler. When an exception is thrown, the runtime examines each stack frame between the throw point and the eventual catch and invokes destructors for objects constructed in those frames in reverse order of construction. This guarantees that resources owned by well-written objects are released, which is the basis for RAII. For a concrete example use the provided MyResource class. If one resource throws while doing work, destructors for previously constructed resources still run and perform their cleanup. A frequent misconception is thinking that raw pointers will be freed automatically; they will not. Only objects with destructors that perform cleanup are invoked during unwinding. In the example, unique_ptr instances hold resources and ensure their destructors call delete. The key takeaway: design destructors to be safe and to perform necessary cleanup because stack unwinding depends on them to keep your program in a valid state. How might you refactor code that currently uses raw new/delete to rely on RAII instead?

Resource Acquisition Is Initialization, or RAII, is the C++ idiom that binds resource lifetime to object lifetime: a constructor acquires a resource and the destructor releases it. Because destructors run during stack unwinding, RAII ensures resources are freed both in normal control flow and when exceptions occur. A common example is file handling: if you open a file and then an exception occurs before you call close, a correctly designed RAII object such as std::fstream or a custom wrapper will close the file in its destructor. The counterexample is manual open and close calls with raw pointers or C file handles — when an exception occurs, the close call may never run and the resource leaks. Use RAII for memory using smart pointers, for locks using lock-guard objects, and for temporary OS resources using small wrapper classes. A common pitfall is writing destructors that can throw; destructors should catch and handle errors internally, perhaps logging failures but not propagating exceptions. Takeaway: prefer RAII everywhere you manage resources so exception paths remain safe and predictable. Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (RAII) means acquire resources in constructors and release them in destructors so cleanup is automatic, even on exceptions.. In practical terms, an idiom for reliable resource management. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparing non-RAII and RAII file handling shows clearly why RAII is preferred. In the non-RAII example you open a file with a raw FILE* and call fclose when you're done. If an exception occurs between the open and close calls, the close call may never execute, and the file handle leaks. In contrast, a RAII wrapper like std::fstream or a custom wrapper opens the file in the constructor and closes it in the destructor. Because destructors are executed during stack unwinding, the file will be closed whether the function finishes normally or an exception propagates. A concrete contrast: imagine a function that performs several operations after opening a file and one of those operations throws. With RAII the file is closed automatically; without RAII it is not. A common misunderstanding is believing that simply adding try/catch around the function will fix leaks — it may, but it complicates code and risks missing other exit paths. RAII centralizes cleanup logic and reduces error-prone bookkeeping. Takeaway: convert manual resource management to RAII to make error handling simpler and safer. Non-RAII vs RAII: file handling means raii centralizes cleanup in destructors so resources are released reliably, while manual open/close is error-prone in the presence of exceptions.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Smart pointers are standard RAII types that manage dynamic memory and free it when the owning object is destroyed. std::unique_ptr models exclusive ownership: only one unique_ptr owns the resource at a time, and its destructor calls delete. Because unique_ptr's destructor runs during stack unwinding, it automatically frees memory even if an exception is thrown. std::shared_ptr models shared ownership: it maintains a reference count and destroys the managed object when the last shared_ptr goes out of scope. A concrete example is creating MyResource instances with std::make_unique; when an exception occurs later, the unique_ptr's destructor invokes delete so memory is reclaimed. A common misconception is that shared_ptr always adds overhead you must avoid; while it has some cost, shared ownership is the right tool for some designs. Another pitfall is mixing raw delete calls with smart pointers — do not manage the same resource with both patterns. Key takeaway: prefer unique_ptr for single ownership and shared_ptr when multiple parts of a program must share a resource, and trust their destructors to provide automatic cleanup in the presence of exceptions. Destructors should generally not throw exceptions. If a destructor throws while another exception is already active—meaning unwinding is in progress—the C++ runtime will call std::terminate and abruptly end the program. This makes throwing from destructors dangerous because it defeats the cleanup guarantees and prevents graceful recovery. Modern C++ implicitly treats destructors as noexcept unless explicitly declared otherwise, which enforces this safety discipline. If a destructor must perform an operation that can fail, handle the failure inside the destructor: log the error, set an internal error state, or swallow the failure quietly in a controlled way. A concrete problematic scenario is calling cleanup code that throws a network error during unwinding; the result would be termination, not an exception you can catch. A common misconception is thinking you can rely on destructor exceptions to propagate useful error information; you cannot. Takeaway: implement destructors to complete non-throwing cleanup, and move any fallible operations to places where failures can be handled without risking termination. The constructor should attempt to create the lock file and throw a LockAcquisitionException if the file already exists, indicating the lock is held. The destructor must be noexcept and should remove the file, handling any failures internally rather than throwing. This checklist gathers common pitfalls and recommended practices for exception-safe C++ code. First, prefer RAII: encapsulate resources in objects whose destructors perform cleanup. Second, use smart pointers for dynamic memory: std::unique_ptr for exclusive ownership, std::shared_ptr when shared semantics are needed. Third, mark destructors noexcept so termination does not occur unexpectedly, and ensure destructors catch and handle internal failures rather than throwing. Fourth, declare move constructors and move assignment noexcept when they do not throw to enable container optimizations. Fifth, avoid mixing raw new/delete with smart pointers and avoid double-management of resources. Sixth, write tests that simulate exceptions during construction and mid-operation so you can confirm cleanup runs during unwinding. A common misconception is that wrapping everything in try/catch everywhere is the right answer — it is not. Instead, design types with strong RAII semantics and let stack unwinding and destructors reliably clean up. Final takeaway: consistent use of RAII and careful noexcept annotations make your code both safer and faster. Which item on this checklist will you apply first in your codebase? Let's summarize the three most important concepts you should carry forward. First, noexcept is a promise that a function will not throw; it helps the compiler optimize and is essential for performance-sensitive move operations, but breaking the promise causes immediate termination. Second, stack unwinding is the runtime mechanism that runs destructors for automatic objects as an exception propagates; it is the foundation that makes RAII effective. Third, RAII ties resource lifetime to object lifetime: acquire resources in constructors and release them in destructors so cleanup is automatic even when exceptions occur. These three concepts combined let you write code that is both efficient and robust in the presence of errors. As you practice with the FileLocker activity, keep these ideas in mind: express non-throwing intent where possible, structure resources as RAII objects, and make destructors non-throwing.

A final set of reminders to use when reviewing or designing code. First, favor std::unique_ptr for single ownership and std::shared_ptr only when sharing is necessary. Second, never allow destructors to throw; handle failures internally and keep destructors effectively noexcept. Third, express non-throwing moves with noexcept so containers can choose more efficient move paths. Use these reminders as quick checks during code review: is this resource managed by an RAII type? Is the destructor non-throwing? Is the move operation marked noexcept when safe? If your answers are yes, your code is likely to be safer and faster. If not, consider refactoring to RAII and adding targeted tests for exception paths.
